newsitem.title: CHINA: Rain,landslips disrupt new HK's first working day.
newsitem.headline: Rain,landslips disrupt new HK's first working day.

text.p: Hong Kong's heaviest rains in 50 years sowed havoc on the territory's first working day under Chinese rule, with floods and landslides blocking roads and badly disrupting public transport as people returned to work.
And more weather chaos was on the way.
Rescue services had to contend with 102 landslides since early Wednesday, and 129 flooding incidents since midnight on Monday when the territory reverted to China, a spokesman said.
A woman trapped in her home under a landslip on Wednesday was still missing.

Landslides severed roads including part of the vital Tuen Mun Highway linking residential new towns in the New Territories region with urban Kowloon, where much of the Hong Kong population work and do business.
The closure forced thousands of people, seeking an alternative route to work, to queue up at a ferry pier.
"At the height of the crowd build-up there were 12,000 people waiting," said police superintendent Albert Ng.
There were also huge traffic jams.
Weather reports said the rain recorded in the past three days was the heaviest in 50 years. In some areas, up to 310 mm (12.4 in) of rain had fallen since Monday, meteorologists said.
"There is a very large amount of rainfall," the government's chief geotechnical engineer Andrew Malone said.
"It now looks as if we had more than 200 square kilometres (75 square miles) of the territory, that's 20 percent of the territory, affected by large amounts of rainfall, 300 milimetres," he said.
Driving rain forced the closure of all schools on Thursday, while courts were also closed in the morning, although they would reopen in the afternoon, the government said.
H.Y. Mok, scientific officer at Hong Kong Observatory, said such heavy rain was "abnormal at this time of the year".
On Wednesday, train services were severely disrupted on the Kowloon Canton Railway because of landslips on the track and passengers had to take shuttle buses instead.
At least eight people were injured in landslides on Wednesday.
A flood of festivities marking the sovereignty transfer was dampened by the foul weather, which forced the cancellation on Wednesday of the territory's biggest ever carnival parade.
It also rained on Britain's farewell parade on Monday night, when the departing colonial power had to hand out thousands of umbrellas to keep the audience dry.
Mok expected the territory to see more heavy rains this week, while authorities also warned of further landslips.
"In terms of what's going to happen in the next 24 hours, we still have intense rain to the south of Hong Kong.
"If that comes back, we will certainly expect more landslips." Malone said.
Sub-tropical Hong Kong's rainy season starts around June and runs through September.

The season often brings ferocious typhoons that can force commuter ferries to suspend services and companies to send their staff home, sometimes for days. No typhoons have struck Hong Kong so far this year.
